title: Runtime Contracts & Safe Tooling Intro - Cobalt Works
summary: Intro demo focused on Redwood JSON mode for structured outputs, safe tool/function calling, and runtime contracts. Customer cares about strong security controls (VPC, KMS, SOC2), deterministic outputs for downstream orchestration, and predictable cost/latency for a pilot. Agreed next steps: share security pack, pilot SOW, and run a two-week benchmark with their sample prompts.
topics: Optimize recommendations for batching and quantization

transcript:
[00:00:00] Jordan (Redwood): hey everyone thanks for joining, looks like we have most folks, um so today we'll run through runtime contracts, json mode, and how tool calling works in a safe way. the session's about 45 minutes plus q&a.
[00:00:30] Maya (Cobalt): hi jordan, thanks. quick context: we're evaluating inferencing platforms for our orchestration layer, main constraints are strict data residency, audit logs, and deterministic structured outputs for downstream systems.
[00:00:55] Jordan: got it, that's exactly what we'll show. sofia's going to demo the console and then we'll look at the api patterns.
[00:01:15] Sofia (Redwood SE): hey all. starting with a quick slide, json mode enforces an output contract based on a schema you provide. if the model returns invalid json, the runtime can auto-correct, or fall back to a parser, or call a recovery tool.
[00:01:40] Liam (Cobalt): when you say "auto-correct" is that lossy? we need exact keys for event processing downstream.
[00:02:05] Sofia: good q. so there are two modes: strict validation which rejects non-conforming outputs and returns an error to the caller, and tolerant mode which tries structured repairs using a repair-toolchain. you can configure per-route policies in the console.
[00:02:35] Priya: and all of that is logged? we need immutable audit trails for anything that manipulates customer PII.
[00:02:50] Jordan: yes, audit logs include original model output, repair attempts, which tool invoked, and the final accepted payload. logs can be retained per your retention policy and exported to your SIEM.
[00:03:10] Sofia: flipping to a short demo now. I'll open the console — bear with me, my network's a bit choppy.
[00:03:40] [screen share starts] Sofia: here is a route configured in json mode. schema attached is a json-schema draft, required fields include user_id, action_type, and metadata. the runtime enforces types and allowed enums.
[00:04:05] Ethan (Cobalt): can we map model slots to our internal ids? like user_id should be numeric int64.
[00:04:25] Sofia: yes, you can declare formats, integer range, even pattern for strings. the schema is how the runtime validates.
[00:04:50] Jordan: a quick note on tool/function calling — you declare callable tools in the console with signatures. the model can be allowed to call them but only after policy checks — e.g., deny network access, or require explicit allowlist.
[00:05:20] Maya: how do you sandbox external tools? we don't want lateral movement if a tool call executes.
[00:05:40] Sofia: good question. tool calls in the hosted product run in an isolated runtime sandbox with strict outbound egress controls. for private/dedicated deployments you can restrict tools to local microservices. also we surface tool call traces in the audit logs.
[00:06:10] [00:06:10] Sofia: here's an example: the model asked to call an inventory_lookup tool, the runtime validated the payload against the tool schema, enforced rate limits, and returned a typed response. if the response didn't match the expected tool schema, the runtime rejected and retried with a fallback.
[00:06:45] Liam: realtime vs async tool responses? some of our internal services are slow.
[00:06:57] Sofia: we support sync and async. for async we return an execution token and publish a webhook when done, or you can poll. policies control timeouts and retries.
[00:07:25] Jordan: let's talk about runtime contracts — these are top-level guarantees you can attach to routes: latency SLO, allowed model families, quantization profiles, and fallback policies.
[00:07:50] Priya: fallback policies — show me an example where a model hallucination could trigger a fallback to a deterministic microservice.
[00:08:10] Sofia: sure. demo snippet: model produced a product_price field as text, schema expects float. runtime detected mismatch, ran the numeric-normalizer tool (deterministic), which corrected and logged the change. we can also configure automatic canary to run deterministic service when confidence is low.
[00:08:45] Maya: confidence scoring, is that model-internal or does your runtime compute it?
[00:08:58] Sofia: runtime computes auxiliary signals (token probabilities, alignment heuristics) plus model-reported confidences where available, then aggregates to decide repairs or fallbacks. there are thresholds you can tune in Optimize.
[00:09:25] Jordan: switching to private deployment considerations — many customers ask about VPC and KMS. we support private control plane with customer-managed VPC peering or on-prem gateways. KMS/HSM integrations are in place for key material.
[00:09:50] Priya: do you provide hardware HSM or only cloud KMS integrations?
[00:10:05] Jordan: we integrate with AWS KMS, GCP KMS, and bring-your-own HSM via standard KMIP. for fully air-gapped setups, our on-prem package can integrate with your HSM.
[00:10:30] Ethan: latency — if we run deterministic fallbacks to our microservices, what's the added 95p?
[00:10:45] Sofia: depends on deployment. in hosted, adding a microservice call in the tool chain adds network RTT; typical extra 95p is 50–150ms if services are colocated in the same region. with Dedicated, you can colocate and see single-digit ms for intra-cluster calls.
[00:11:10] [00:11:10] Sofia: demo continues — showing schema versioning: you can pin a schema to a model version, do gradual rollouts, and if a model upgrade breaks schema conformance we can automatically rollback to prior model.
[00:11:40] Maya: that's great. our main concern: models change outputs subtly and break downstream parsers.
[00:11:55] Jordan: exactly why runtime contracts exist. they let you decouple model rollouts from application rollouts.
[00:12:20] Liam: any built-in evals for schema regression? like run a suite of prompts and fail on breaking changes?
[00:12:35] Sofia: yes, Optimize includes prompt sets / eval harness that can assert schema conformance and output quality. it will produce a regression report and optional alerting.
[00:12:55] Priya: security review — we need SOC2 type ii, ISO 27001, SAML SSO, RBAC, and detailed audit logs. do you have those docs?
[00:13:15] Jordan: we do. I'll send the full security pack. we have SOC2 report, ISO attestation, SSO integrations (SAML/OIDC), and fine-grained RBAC for console and API keys.
[00:13:40] Maya: and for data residency — can we keep logs in our GCP project or do they flow through Redwood?
[00:13:55] Jordan: with Private you run the control plane in your VPC and store logs to your destination. For Hosted we offer regionally isolated storage and export hooks.
[00:14:20] Sofia: back to tooling — showing function signatures. you can set schemas for tool inputs and outputs. the model must adhere to the output contract. we also have a sandbox 'dry-run' that prevents state changes during testing.
[00:14:50] Ethan: is there a simulator to test model-to-tool interactions locally?
[00:15:05] Sofia: yes, the SDK includes a local simulator that mirrors runtime validation rules. it helps iterate before deploying to staging.
[00:15:30] Jordan: a common ask: cost controls. Optimize will analyze your token profile and suggest batching sizes, kv caching configs, and whether quantization is viable for a given workload.
[00:15:55] Maya: can optimize suggest quantization profiles safely for our SMEs? we worry about small quality regressions.
[00:16:10] Sofia: Optimize runs A/B tests on historical prompts and reports delta in output quality. you set acceptance criteria and it will only recommend quant profiles that meet thresholds.
[00:16:35] Liam: what's 'kv cash' in the docs? (laughter)
[00:16:45] Jordan: (laughs) kv cache, yes. the runtime manages KV cache for prefixes to reduce repeated tokens, that helps latency and cost on conversational workloads.
[00:17:10] [00:17:10] Sofia: moving to a live example of a tool fallback chain. I fire a prompt that asks the model to provide a shipping ETA. the model replies with "ETA: two weeks" which doesn't match the expected ISO date format. runtime triggers date-normalizer tool, which converts to 2027-02-01 and annotates the payload with a reason code. logs show original and normalized.
[00:17:45] Maya: can we add business rules to normalizers? e.g. if ETA > 30 days escalate to manual review.
[00:17:58] Sofia: yes, policy engine supports conditional logic and can trigger manual approval flows or route to human-in-the-loop.
[00:18:20] Priya: are those manual steps auditable? we need chain-of-custody.
[00:18:30] Jordan: every step is recorded: who approved, when, and what changes were applied.
[00:18:50] Liam: latency and cost — if we enable tight validation and run multiple repair tools per request, that could balloon cost. any recommendations?
[00:19:10] Sofia: yes, Optimize suggests policy mixes: e.g., strict validation for payment routes (fail-fast) and tolerant plus caching for low-risk routes. it will model cost impact and show per-request delta.
[00:19:40] [00:19:40] Sofia: I'll switch to API examples now — here's a simple POST to /v1/respond with route=shipments-json. Notice the request includes schema_version and a tools_allowed list.
[00:20:05] Jordan: we also support streaming typed responses so you can start processing partial validated JSON chunks while the model streams the rest.
[00:20:25] Maya: any caveats with streaming and schema enforcement?
[00:20:40] Sofia: the runtime validates chunks incrementally — if a later chunk causes schema break, you get an error and a recovery option. streaming is best for responsiveness but requires careful client handling.
[00:21:05] Ethan: about function calls — can we restrict which models can call which tools? we have some models we trust more.
[00:21:20] Sofia: yes, model-to-tool allowlists are configurable per route and per environment.
[00:21:40] Liam: curious about testing — do you support fuzzing the schema to find edge cases?
[00:21:55] Sofia: Optimize has a fuzzing module that generates variants of prompts and malformed outputs to check parser robustness.
[00:22:15] Jordan: quick pivot — procurement and timelines, what are you thinking for pilot scope and timeline?
[00:22:30] Maya: we'd like a two-week pilot focusing on two routes: shipments and returns, with deterministic fallbacks enabled for shipments. timeline: start Feb 1, procurement signoff by Jan 27.
[00:22:55] Jordan: ok we'll prepare SOW and a pilot config.
[00:23:15] Priya: one more: pen-test requirements? we require external pen-test and ability to provide remediation windows.
[00:23:30] Jordan: we can coordinate that, we have a standard pen-test process and will share the schedule.
[00:23:50] Sofia: demo wrap-up, tl;dr: json mode + schemas let you lock outputs, tool calling is typed and auditable, runtime contracts manage rollouts and fallbacks, Optimize gives guardrail recommendations.
[00:24:10] Maya: thanks, that helped. couple of quick clarifications on who to expect emails from.
[00:24:25] Jordan: I'll send the security pack and SOW. Sofia will provision the pilot workspace. Maya will send prompt sets.
[00:24:40] [Crosstalk as participants exchange calendar invites]
[00:25:05] Jordan: any other questions?
[00:25:20] Liam: when we run the benchmark, can we get per-token cost breakdown by model variant?
[00:25:35] Sofia: yes, console shows token-level cost, latency percentiles, and breakdown by route and model.
[00:25:55] Priya: do you have an SLA for hosted versus dedicated?
[00:26:10] Jordan: hosted has best-effort, dedicated comes with SLA targets for uptime and tail latency per contract. we'll include SLA options in the SOW.
[00:26:35] Maya: for the pilot, we'd prefer dedicated to avoid noisy-neighbor concerns.
[00:26:50] Jordan: noted, we'll include dedicated pricing.
[00:27:05] Sofia: last demo note — developer ergonomics: SDKs include typed clients that enforce schema and tool signatures at compile time, reducing mismatches before runtime.
[00:27:30] Ethan: nice. that will help our platform team.
[00:27:45] Jordan: ok let's recap next steps.
[00:28:00] [recap] Jordan: 1) send security pack and SOC2 — jordan; 2) pilot SOW + dedicated pricing — jordan; 3) provision pilot workspace with json-mode templates — sofia; 4) customer to share prompts and access requirements — maya.
[00:28:25] Maya: thanks everyone, we'll review and aim for procurement signoff by Jan 27.
[00:28:40] [00:28:40] Jordan: great, talk soon.
[00:52:50] [call ended]
venue_notes: Recorded via Fireflies; screen-share demo included. Customer provided sample prompt-set link (not pasted) and attached security questionnaire during call.
